records.videoTitle: Episode 34 - Construction vs Service and The Different TYPES of Electrical Work You Can Do
records.commentText: I probably won’t get an answer since this is a big channel but I am just curious what do you consider is better for the learning experience? New construction or service electrical. If you see this get back to me please
records.threadText: Reply 1: In order to do service you must be first acquainted with construction. The apprenticeship prospectus is designed this way. Are you already an apprentice or wanting to be one? And what do you mean by best learning experience? The most technical work is learning to troubleshoot broken systems, smartly diagnosing and coming up with a quick prognosis because the employer wants a quick remedy to the problem to reactivate production. That extra little bit of learning experience will come with service industrial (maintenance) and commercial. On the other hand, opening a residential business is better learning experience as it predisposes you to the rigors of creating a business, skills not taught in the electrical trade but expected to be mastered on one's own.

records.videoTitle: Should you pigtail your electrical outlets? The answer might surprise you.
records.commentText: I was taught to Pig-tail in my training . My recollection is that there was a code reqyirement that removing a device not interupt the neutrual. Reducing the number of conductors to the device makes for easier device instal lation into the box and reduces the number of screw terminals that may loosen over time as well.
records.threadText:
Reply 1: I’ve been a licensed electrician for almost four decades and there is no code requirement for pigtails. It’s optional. We pigtail often with industrial work or even in commercial installations but I almost never see pigtails in residential. But like I said in the video there are applications where it makes sense. If you like that method of course stick with it.
Reply 2: Nec 300.13 (B)
Reply 3: That's just for the neutral on multiwire branch circuits. I mentioned that in the video. 
300.13 Mechanical and Electrical Continuity, Conductors
(A) General
Conductors in raceways shall be continuous between outlets, boxes, devices, and so forth. There shall be no splice or tap within a raceway unless permitted by 300.15, 368.56(A), 376.56, 378.56, 384.56, 386.56, 388.56, or 390.56.
(B) Device Removal
In multiwire branch circuits, the continuity of a grounded conductor shall not depend on device connections such as lampholders, receptacles, and so forth, where the removal of such devices would interrupt the continuity.@@waxphantomscousin8278
Reply 4: So for all 240 volt, or 3 wire Romex where you're running 2 parallel 120V circuits you have to pigtail the neutral, no exceptions? In that case, 240V outlets in garages cannot use the pass through on neutrals?@@BackyardMaine
Reply 5: @@starseeddeluxe A multi-wire branch circuit supplies line to neutral loads only. A 240v circuit supplies line to line loads and often times requires a neutral for line to neutral load on the make equipment. (lights etc.. When you run a three wire to supply 120v receptacles where both hot conductors return on the one neutral thats considered multi-wire and the neutral cannot feed through the device. 300.13 (B) and 210.4

Reply 3: @@jamescody9982 Good question. Most residential applications will have a plastic or fiberglass box and the ground wire needs to ground the switch yoke. The metal frame of the switch. records.videoTitle: How to bend and install electrical conduit
records.commentText:
Great video! Electrician here as well. Just a little 2 cents for anyone interested; since he was using 1/2 inch pipe, the take up (or deduction, the part you subtract when bending a 90 on the arrow) was 5". However, keep in mind, that these change from size to size. So if you're using 3/4" , the deduction is 6". If you're using 1", the deduction is 8". As he said in the video, it will be listed on the bender. Also, if you don't want to do the deduction, you can do something called "bending on center". Usually this is denoted on the bender by a star, and this allows you to just mark your exact measurement, and line the mark up with the star, as opposed to the arrow. Just a little less math involved is all. 
I work mainly commercial, but most of this information was very useful for anyone just starting off/doing a home project. This is stuff i only learned after being at many sites. I've never seen those bracket 1900s though, those are pretty nice!

an offset of 15 degrees, you multiply the height of your offset by 3.8

an offset of 45 degrees, you multiply the height of your offset by 1.4
example for an offset of 3 inches at 30 degrees you multiply 3'' X 2
so it will be 6 inches in both marks where the conduit will be bent at 30 degrees.

records.commentText: Why does water trip circuits even if it is only in contact with a live wire only or a neutral wire only?
records.threadText: Reply 1: t rex I’m not sure I understand your question. If the water is touching ground or anything connected to ground, then there will be a voltage between the water and the live wire, so when they touch, a large current will flow and trip the switch. If the return wire is disconnected from the neutral terminal, then it could be live (if that circuit is switched on) and it too will trip the switch when connected to the water. However, if the water came into contact with the neutral terminal, nothing would happen because there would not be a voltage between the water and the neutral terminal.

records.commentText: I am a carpenter. And we were doing a demo job, which included gutting a kitchen. And our electricians had to move lights, add outlets, add switches, and segregate lights. But the drywall was already up. And couldn’t rip it apart. How do electricians feed wire thru a wall without being able to get in from the attic or remove the drywall???
records.threadText:
Reply 1: kyle blume I worked new residential electrical for a while and we cut “transfers” in the Sheetrock at studs to drill through the stud and fish, then run the wire through.. after installation or running, we would screw the piece we cut out back onto the stud and the sheet rockers would patch the cracks..
Reply 2: The guys that did our drywall didn’t cut any drywall aside from the new sockets being installed. And the new round holes for light cans in the ceiling.
Reply 3: kyle blume gotcha, the ceiling was probably the easier of the two.. they do make extremely long drill bits that allow us to hook a wire on the end of and drill through Walls, Joyce’s, and fire blocks.. it’s a lot of hard work though, not cutting or removing Sheetrock when moving runs or plugs and switches.. depending on how far the relocation is of course.. if it was only a couple inches to a foot of moving around it’s doable from the “Demo hole” from removing the fixture or outlet.
Reply 4: Of course Dustin could give you the proper technical terms and ideology behind how we go about doing things like that!😂

records.videoTitle: Electrical Wire Color Coding Used By Electricians
records.commentText: Really appreciate these videos. I am not an electrician, but do some of my own work. Great to see these videos targeted with simple explanations. So many “electricians” really have no clue what they are doing.
records.threadText:
Reply 1: True, lol! Always, ALWAYS double check. Have a LICENSED person check and double check. 
And follow around anyone in your house like you're a dog and they have Milk Bones in their pockets...get a guy that likes to talk and explains everything well. 
Pay them extremely well and tip in cash if you call and they're there right away. 
Look out for places that hire some idiot off the street to work for you who doesn't know wtf they're doing and has no license.
Reply 2: The city doesn't tell you what colors you have to use for the current carrying conductors. The code specifies for the grounded conductor (neutral) it is to me identified as white or grey with that being the color of the insulation on the wire or wrapped with tape of that color at any assible point, like a junction box. Usually we like to use white tape for 120/240 single phase systems and 120/208 3 phase systems and grey wire or tape for the neutral in 277/480 v olt 3 phase systems. For the grounding conductor we use green color insulation or green marking tape regardless of the voltage of the system. So foreign and European equipment use green insulation with a yellow stripe.
Reply 3: @@jtd2949Code (NEC) says that 6AWG neutrals (grounded conductor) or smaller shall be solid white or grey, phase tape allowed on larger wire that doesn’t come in colors.

records.videoTitle: Electrical Work Ep.97
records.commentText: Are you going to do anything with data lines?
records.threadText:
Reply 1: Fiber throughout the house would be excellent. Hope they do it.
Reply 2: Good question. I would and did wire my whole house for data using several different cable types (e.g. Ethernet, Coax, fiber). And, even though wireless may be a thing, I'd still do hard wire with multi purpose outlets. I'd also overdo the number of 120V outlets wherever electronics might be used. I know it's expensive, but worth it in the long run.
Reply 3: @@susanbarbier5053 I think Cat 6 for most of the house will be fine. Fiber is not necessary and actually hurts resale. Ever seen the cost of Fiber network gear and the connectors. You need a LOT of money to deal with Fiber. Cat6/Cat6a can do 10 Gbps up and down. That means you are looking at moving a multiple Gig files in minutes. The only difference between 6 and 6a is data run length. 6 can handle 50 meters runs max with 6a handling 100 meters.
Reply 4: @@jacksak 
>And, even though wireless may be a thing
Hate dealing with it, tbh. Both my parents and my aunt have issues with getting a good wifi signal in some parts of their houses. Now mind you, this is German brick and mortar construction, with some steel in it, but you can also have everyday electronic devices messing with your wifi signal.
Reply 5: @@urishima Yes, I understand. I never liked the idea of wireless due to reception and security issues.
Also, as for electrical interference, I'm retired now, but was responsible for data wire layouts in New York City and other locations working for an international company. I worked with union electricians and others making sure the job was done right (and no interference).
In the 1980's union electricians didn't know how to install and wire connections for data. So, on several sites, we paid off local electricians who then allowed our guys to do the connections while the electricians went to the local bar... no kidding and no joke. It happened among many other unbelievable things.
Once, on a large commercial building site where non-union data wire guys were installing our cable to 100+ terminal locations all trunked into a computer room, the electricians cut the trunk of 100+ cables as it came into the computer room. Each line then had to be buzzed out to figure out how to reconnect/splice the cable back together.
Dozens more stories that seem unbelievable but happened...

records.threadText: Reply 1: This is the rough in. Lasers dont mean jack. You can square up and accurately position lights with a measuring tape and a few other traditional tools. Lasers help, but they are not intrinsically more helpful than a square for example. Also, notice the extra length of cable fed into the cans? Why do you speak on things you clearly don't understand. GFCI protection is ground independent and NO GROUND IS REQUIRED for GFCI protection. Period. If you have three-prong receptacles, then it's dangerous if there is no actual ground because the device you're plugging in is designed for protective ground if it has a three-prong plug. Reply 4: @@2Truth4Liberty Don't listen to this fraud. GFCI protects downstream devices and no ground is required. Period. You need to be very careful, though, that there is no other neutral path downstream or the GFCI will trip every time since both the HOT and Neutral need to be connected only to the GFCI on the LOAD side.

records.commentText: Is there a specific amp fuse I should be using or could I get away with all 10s or whatever? I bought a boat used that is pre wired but just missing fuses. Wondering if I have to look up the bilge, and LEDs and find the specific fuse they want?
records.threadText:
Reply 1: The fuse should be rated to the cable current rating or lower.
The cable current rating should be equal or higher than the appliance current rating.
Design procedure:
1. Decide on what devices/loads you are going to connect to the single circuit.
2. Calculate the maximum power dissipation of the loads. Translate this into amps. (Using I = P/V)
3. Set the cable current rating to be higher. Identify what thickness (or cross sectional area cable you need).
4. Select the fuse rating to be equal or less than the cable rating but higher than the maximum load current determined in step 2.
Reply 2: What Dean G said, just lower than the wire is rated for. I usually do 5s and 10s
Reply 3: @@SendItJonBoats Where you have a an extension lead providing power to a single appliance:
There is a fuse in the plug of the appliance whose value is set by the manufacturer. That protects the appliance cable and the appliance.
The setting of the fuse in the extension lead plug is not for the benefit of the appliance, it is to protect the extension cable.
It serves no benefit whatsoever to lower that fuse to the same rating as the appliance fuse.

records.commentText:
I went to community college right after graduating high school (I finish my AA program in two months). I did it for my parents but now, I'm finally taking a serious look at myself and realizing that higher education doesn't fit my talents and personality. I love intense physical exercise and working long hours in settings that are at least somewhat physical; I used to do 30-40 hours a week at Taco Bell on top of working out 2 hours a day and it kinda "distracted me" from the loneliness and stress I got from college studying.
Even though I have no prior knowledge or connections with anyone who's an electrician, there's an affordable and fairly rigorous program close to home that I spoke with and it sounds like exactly what I want out of life. It looks like you reply to a lot of comments so I want to ask: What could I expect from a 1-year electrician program that gets me ready for a state test? What kind of tasks would I do on a daily basis? Is it possible that they'll give me some kind of high order math (like algebra) to study as part of the curriculum? 
Any answer or reply will help me. Thank you and God bless.

records.videoTitle: Complete Solar Panel Connection with Solar Charge Controller and Inverter @TheElectricalGuy
records.commentText: Sir can't some one use only the panel controller and battery only?
records.threadText:
Reply 1: If you are asking if it is mandatory to connect your load circuits to the controller to make panels charge up your batteries, then the answer is no. As an example, if you had panel(s) and controller hooked up to your battery bank and then the lights in your RV connected as load, if no lights were turned on, your batteries would charge up just fine. The advantage of connecting your actual load circuits to the controller is that Bluetooth enabled controller can give you some valuable measurements about your whole system. You may discover, for example, that a circuit you thought had a very low power draw may, in fact, be responsible for depleting your battery bank faster than you thought it would. There are a lot of 12 VDC devices that are intended for use in an automotive application and when the vehicle is running, they can draw heavy current and the alternator will keep the start battery charged fully. A car radio or CD player might be an example of a device that could deplete your battery bank very quickly. Although inverter manufacturers say you can run your inverter 24/7, there is nothing wrong with turning it off if you want zero current draw to occur. My modest true sine wave inverter came equipped with a corded on/off switch and, most days, I only turn it on to grind my coffee beans for breakfast coffee. A laptop computer is generally not a battery killer, and you can keep an eye on the laptop battery gauge, and only start using a 120VAC power pack to bring it back up to 100% when it gets low. A 120VAC heating device of any sort is a real power glutton. For this reason, refrigerators are best operated on propane and ideally, one that does NOT require 12 VDC to run the propane function. I was fortunate to find a second-hand "passive" refrigerator that had a freezer compartment and it requires no 12 VDC to operate. Shower water heaters that use batteries or 12 VDC to ignite only use power when water flows and the burner needs to be ignited. I like the 12 VDC flat two (like trailer running light connectors) since I have seen problems with the battery door failing to make good connections on water heaters of fellow campers. It takes very little to connect a 12 VDC power cord to the water heater. The display circuit on mine only operates on demand when water flows.
Reply 2: On the topic of powering your laptop, I find it better to use a 12 VDC cigar lighter power cord for my Lenovo Think Pad laptop so the inverter colling fan will not run when the laptop is drawing a heavy current. My Lenovo cord was over $50 but standard-rated 3.1 amp USB receptacle to USB-C cord arrangements are underpowered and fail to be recognized as an acceptable power input for that Lenovo laptop. 
If your laptop requires a DC voltage greater than 12 VDC, there are inexpensive voltage raising circuit boards that work fine. You just have to fine tune the output voltage when they are applied. I have had complete success with this approach.

records.commentText: Only question I have....always been told to have the breaker OFF when plugging in the RV. I know you plugged the RV into the surge protector, but does the surge protector provide the same precaution as having the 30 amp breaker off when plugging in? Make sense?
records.threadText:
Reply 1: The breaker does not need to be turned off before plugging the RV in. Just like the breakers in your home dont have to be switched on and off every time you plug your vacuum in.
Reply 2: @@FateUnbound David, the reason why its best the breaker should be turned off when you plug or unplug the RV power cord, is any load whatsoever (albeit small, present in some devices like a charger or one having a inductive or capacitor load even if turned off) can still cause some degree of arcing which can create resistive carbon or pitting or burning (ever look at your RV power cord plug ??) on the contacts PLUS its safer when plugging or unplugging if the breaker is off. That's NOT just me saying that, I've owned RV's 49 years and heard that long ago.
John T BSEE,JD Retired Electrical Power Distribution Design Engineer

records.videoTitle: 30 Amp RV Outlet Install - DIY Electrical Receptacle Wiring
records.commentText:
Excellent video, good information, and good pacing to illustrate the project effectively. As a licensed home inspector in NC, my only concern is that *if* you did not unplug the trailer from the 15 amp service, you may have energized the main panel when the generator was started for the work tools. I am sure that you did unplug, but that is the only omission I can see. Terrific work and explanation of the process! 
An identical 30A outlet was added under my parents' porch a couple of years ago, and my sisters and I use it with our trailers when visiting. Before that, one sister's trailer was tripping the garage GFCI circuit. Last year, after the parents lost a TV, perhaps a refrigerator, and needed a new control board in a 5 year-old HVAC air handler, I installed a Square D/Schneider whole-house surge protector in the main panel. So that also protects the RV outlet. So far so good!
records.threadText:
Reply 1: *Inverter, not generator
Agree with previous comments that a strain relief should be used where the new Romex enters the main panel, missed that.
Neutrals and grounds may be landed in separate bus bars in main panels, but they are still connected. It is in sub panels that they are electrically isolated.

records.videoTitle: Episode 35 - Day 1 of Your Electrical Career - How To Be A Great Apprentice
records.commentText:
I'm a first year plumber apprentice and the journeymen that work with me hate me. I rag on how slow they move and how they're teaching me wrong. How they don't take responsibility for directing me leading to errors.
This isn't a career for me, just a job. One day, hopefully soon, I'll be laid off and able to run my side business full time.
Worst points about the apprenticeship. Lazy ass journeymen. I get that apprentices' need to learn how to do the job, but not the housekeeping and moving shit because the journeymen is old, fat, or just straight up lazy. We are a 1:1 team and if we make a mess, we clean it up together.
Journeymen have the final and only words. I break this all the time. No one is going to walk all over me and dismiss critical points I bring up about certain jobs around the site. Everyone always say, "Ask questions" and when I do I'm treated like I won't understand it, or I didn't hear it.
The constant "safety meetings" and the PPE.
Imagine starting a day off. Arriving 15 minutes early and standing around the guys and your journeymen walks up and starts giving you orders. I tell him we aren't on the clock so I can't help him yet. It is now time to work, I grab my tools and his and ask if there is anything else we need and that I will bring it all up for him so we can start working. He will ignore me so I proceed to take our tools and some materials to the work area. I start the daily task plan and he walks up and tells me to hurry. And asks for "XYZ" material that he didn't tell me to get. Then turns walking away grumbling "useless 1st years" or the similar...Now imagine going through that daily while wearing an annoying neck scratching reflective vest. Safety glasses that will fog up hindering your eye sight when doing the most crucial part of the task and a big ass hard hat that slips off, slides down, won't tighten up, gets knocked off from moving around the job.
Yeah...entrepreneurship is my career.
records.threadText:
Reply 1: Stick with it, this is life pushing you to your limits. Man once you learn to get over the small petty things going on in life right now, you'll reap the bigger benefits soon to come. Think of what you're going through as an initiation phase. You keep up your persistence, don't sweat the small stuff and do as you're told. You'll be the happiest apprentice less than 8 months from now. 
 Quit now, start your business, go through even more trial and error (that's gonna be capable of putting you out of business for years) rushing to the money, you'll never be quite satisfied. Learn the things life wants to teach you today(humble yourself), life tomorrow teaching life a thing or two.

Worst points about the apprenticeship. Lazy ass journeymen. I get that apprentices' need to learn how to do the job, but not the housekeeping and moving shit because the journeymen is old, fat, or just straight up lazy. We are a 1:1 team and if we make a mess, we clean it up together.
Journeymen have the final and only words. I break this all the time. No one is going to walk all over me and dismiss critical points I bring up about certain jobs around the site. Everyone always say, "Ask questions" and when I do I'm treated like I won't understand it, or I didn't hear it.
The constant "safety meetings" and the PPE.
Imagine starting a day off. Arriving 15 minutes early and standing around the guys and your journeymen walks up and starts giving you orders. I tell him we aren't on the clock so I can't help him yet. It is now time to work, I grab my tools and his and ask if there is anything else we need and that I will bring it all up for him so we can start working. He will ignore me so I proceed to take our tools and some materials to the work area. I start the daily task plan and he walks up and tells me to hurry. And asks for "XYZ" material that he didn't tell me to get. Then turns walking away grumbling "useless 1st years" or the similar...Now imagine going through that daily while wearing an annoying neck scratching reflective vest. Safety glasses that will fog up hindering your eye sight when doing the most crucial part of the task and a big ass hard hat that slips off, slides down, won't tighten up, gets knocked off from moving around the job.
Yeah...entrepreneurship is my career.

REPLIES:
Reply 1: Stick with it, this is life pushing you to your limits. Man once you learn to get over the small petty things going on in life right now, you'll reap the bigger benefits soon to come. Think of what you're going through as an initiation phase. You keep up your persistence, don't sweat the small stuff and do as you're told. You'll be the happiest apprentice less than 8 months from now. 
 Quit now, start your business, go through even more trial and error (that's gonna be capable of putting you out of business for years) rushing to the money, you'll never be quite satisfied. Learn the things life wants to teach you today(humble yourself), life tomorrow teaching life a thing or two.

records.commentText: The various lever connectors have the same issue you mentioned in another video about back stabbing an outlet. The connection relies on spring tension, and the surface area of contact is relatively small compared to a twisted connection covered by a wire nut, or by side wiring the outlet. Tests have shown that the lever connectors have higher resistance and create more heat, thus making them inferior for high current connections. Every type of connector has it's place, and I don't believe anyone should be claiming lever nuts are the best approach for all things. Just my humble opinion.
records.threadText:
Reply 1: They are designed for a specific current. Use for that and it is perfectly safe.
Reply 2: I think most lever nuts don't use spring tension like the quick connectors on an outlet. They make like 2 line connectors that use the same principle as those but the lever designs don't. As someone who isn't a skilled electrician I am starting to swap to lever connectors because they are brain dead easy to use. I don't have to worry if I did the lines perfect for the wire nut when connecting stranded to solid or w.e. They are simple and plug and play as it were. Most of my electrical work is changing light fixtures or switches so nothing high load. The levers shouldn't ever have an issue with those and the increased resistance is non existent especially because my house was build in the 80s so with everything being LED lighting these days the load is even less.
